one_line: Better Stack walkthrough of OpenAI's new Python Agents SDK: agents, handoffs via a router agent, function and built-in tools, local context, input guardrails, and built-in tracing.
summary: The video builds a small travel assistant with OpenAI's Python Agents SDK, which was Python-only at release (a JavaScript version was expected). It defines two specialist agents (a city info agent and a flight finder agent) plus a router agent that hands requests off to them using handoff descriptions and a recommended prompt prefix. It then adds tools: the built-in web search tool, a plain Python function turned into a tool with a decorator, and a Pydantic local context object passed through the runner. An input guardrail runs a small classifier agent to reject non-trip-planning requests, and the presenter notes that guardrails only run on the starting agent. The video closes by showing the agent runs in OpenAI's platform traces view. It is a practical hands-on tutorial with no benchmarks.

key_ideas.idea: Agents are an LLM with its own instructions and tools, and each agent can use a different model, so a specialized task can get the best model for it.
key_ideas.detail: Two logic agents (city info, flight finder) differ only in name, instructions and model. The presenter uses a routine-style instruction pattern from OpenAI demos: if a request falls outside the routine, hand it back.

key_ideas.idea: Multi-agent routing uses a triage/router agent that delegates through handoffs, with each specialist's capabilities described in its handoff description.
key_ideas.detail: The router's handoffs list holds the specialists. Each specialist gets a handoff description so the router knows what it can do, rather than putting that in the router's instructions. Every handoff-enabled agent gets the recommended prompt prefix from the SDK package.

key_ideas.idea: Specialists can hand back to the router by appending it to their handoffs list after it is defined, since the router is declared last.
key_ideas.detail: Because the router is defined after the other agents, the presenter adds it to each agent's handoffs list afterward instead of in the constructor. The router also needs its own handoff description.

key_ideas.idea: The runner takes a starting agent and an input list, and the result's new items show intermediate steps like tool calls and handoffs.
key_ideas.detail: The runner exposes run, run sync and run streamed. Input is the conversation so far (user input plus LLM output). Printing final_output gives only the answer; iterating new_items shows which tools ran and which agents were handed off to.

key_ideas.idea: Tools can be built-in (web search) or any Python function wrapped with the function_tool decorator, which takes the name, description and argument docs from the function.
key_ideas.detail: Adding the built-in web search tool is one line in the tools list. A custom weather function becomes a tool with function_tool, and its name, docstring and argument descriptions are read automatically.

key_ideas.idea: Local context is a typed object (a Pydantic model here) passed to runner.run and read or written by tools. It is not sent to the LLM.
key_ideas.detail: Tools receive it wrapped in a run context wrapper and read it as wrapper.context. The presenter suggests a generic type parameter on the agent so all tools in one run share the same context type. Good for user names, helpers, loggers and fetch clients.

key_ideas.idea: Input guardrails run in parallel with the agent. A guardrail agent with structured output can trip a wire to stop the run when the request is off-topic.
key_ideas.detail: The guardrail returns a tripwire flag, and when it is set the SDK raises an input-guardrail-tripwire exception that can be caught to return a message. The guardrail only runs on the starting agent, so it must be attached to each specialist that should enforce it.

key_ideas.idea: Built-in tracing records each run as an agent workflow in the provider dashboard, showing handoffs, tool calls and their arguments.
key_ideas.detail: The presenter opens the OpenAI platform traces tab and inspects a city info run that was handed off to the router. This is the main debugging aid the video highlights.

techniques.name: Router/triage agent with handoff descriptions
techniques.how: Create specialist agents with a name, instructions, a model, tools and a handoff_description. Create a router agent whose handoffs list holds the specialists. Prepend the SDK's recommended prompt prefix to every handoff-enabled agent's instructions. If a specialist must return unhandled requests, define the router after the specialists and append it to their handoffs list afterwards.
techniques.when: Splitting one assistant into domain specialists where the routing decision should be made by an LLM from the specialist descriptions.

techniques.name: Function tool from a Python function
techniques.how: Decorate a plain Python function with the SDK's function_tool directive. Write a docstring for the tool description and per-argument descriptions. Add the decorated function to the agent's tools list. The name comes from the function name and the input schema is generated automatically.
techniques.when: Exposing your own API or logic (for example a weather lookup) to an agent without writing a JSON schema by hand.

techniques.name: Typed local context object
techniques.how: Define a Pydantic model for per-run state such as user name or city. Pass an instance to runner.run as the third argument. In tools, read or write wrapper.context. Add the context type as a generic parameter on the agent so every tool in that run uses the same type.
techniques.when: Carrying request-scoped data like user identity, helpers, loggers or clients into tools without putting them in the prompt.

techniques.name: Guardrail as a classifier agent
techniques.how: Write an input guardrail function that takes context, agent and input. Inside it, run a small agent via the runner with a structured output type, such as a boolean field plus a reasoning string. Return a guardrail result with tripwire_triggered set when the classifier rejects the input. Attach the guardrail to the agent's input_guardrails list, and catch the tripwire exception to return a user-facing error.
techniques.when: Keeping a purpose-built assistant on topic, for example refusing general chat in a trip planner.

techniques.name: Inspecting run steps with new_items
techniques.how: After runner.run returns, iterate over result.new_items instead of printing only final_output. Each item shows tool calls, tool outputs and handoffs.
techniques.when: Debugging multi-agent routing during development before turning on hosted tracing.

hot_takes: Guardrails only run on the starting agent, so a guardrail on the router does not protect specialists reached by handoff. The presenter calls this a gotcha and says the docs explain it by saying guardrails are tied to individual agents.
The presenter says the guardrail was needed because a deployed tool was being used as a free general chatbot.
The SDK is Python-only at this point, and the video says a JavaScript version might come later.

relevance.why: AgentOS sits in front of agents as a proxy, so the SDK's guardrail and tracing patterns are conceptually adjacent to the L1 scan and observability layers, but the video only covers the SDK's own features and shows no proxy integration.
relevance.action: Compare the SDK's input guardrail model (per-agent, runs only on the starting agent) with the proxy-level PII and prompt-injection scan, and note that proxy checks apply to every request while SDK guardrails are per-agent.

relevance.why: Handoffs between a router and specialist agents map loosely onto ProsHarness's plan, critique and debate flow, but the video only covers LLM-routed delegation, not checkpointing or resumable runs.
relevance.action: Skim the handoff and new_items model as a reference for how ProsHarness could record which sub-agent produced each step in a checkpoint.
